summary: Defines how CAPWAP is used with IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs, so a central Access Controller can manage wireless termination points in a standard way. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: This is the chapter for managing wifi boxes specifically. It says how the boss computer's general orders apply to ordinary wifi.

subtitle: How a central controller manages IEEE 802.11 wireless access points over CAPWAP, in Split MAC and Local MAC modes.

tldr.problem: The CAPWAP protocol (RFC 5415) lets a central Access Controller manage wireless termination points but deliberately contains nothing specific to any radio technology. A binding is needed for IEEE 802.11.
tldr.mechanism: This binding assigns wireless binding identifier 1, divides 802.11 functions between the controller (AC) and the access point (WTP) in Split MAC or Local MAC mode, and defines two control messages, 25 message elements, QoS handling and key refresh procedures.
tldr.outcome: A controller can configure WLANs, stations, radios and security on 802.11 access points in a standard way. It supports only IEEE 802.11-2007, with no ad hoc mode and no official 802.11n support.

today: RFC 5416 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5415, and the text itself says newer IEEE amendments such as 802.11n need a separate binding or an update to this one.

sections.title: Why a Binding for 802.11
sections.content:
Wireless LAN products have evolved from single autonomous access points to systems made of a centralized Access Controller (AC) and Wireless Termination Points (WTPs). The goal is to move access control, including user authentication and authorization, mobility management and radio management, from each access point to the central controller.

The CAPWAP protocol (RFC 5415) is wireless agnostic and relies on a binding specification for each radio technology. This document is the binding for IEEE 802.11. It uses wireless binding identifier 1 in the CAPWAP header.

The scope is narrow on purpose. The binding supports only IEEE 802.11-2007, not the ad hoc mode and not four-address wireless bridge frames. It does not officially support IEEE 802.11n: a WTP may advertise an 802.11n radio, but none of the additional features can be configured or used. It requires the Wi-Fi Alliance WPA and WMM specifications. It covers only the interface between a WTP and its AC, not inter-AC or station-to-AC communication.
sections.eli5: CAPWAP is a general rulebook for a boss computer and its helper boxes. This chapter adds the special rules for wifi helper boxes.

sections.title: Split MAC and Local MAC
sections.content:
Which device does what depends on the mode. In both modes the CAPWAP functions reside in the AC. The WTP and AC MUST support 802.11 encryption and decryption at the WTP, and MAY support it at the AC.

In Split MAC, the distribution and integration services live on the AC, so all user data is tunneled between WTP and AC. The WTP handles real-time work such as Beacon and Probe Response frames and packet buffering. Association handling, 802.1X/EAP and key management are on the AC, which means the AAA client is there too.

In Local MAC, the integration service is on the WTP, and the distribution service MAY be on either side. Because the MAC ends at the WTP, the WTP MUST still forward Association Request frames to the AC. The AC MAY answer with a failed Association Response, and then the WTP MUST send a Disassociation frame to the station. The WTP MUST forward all 802.1X, EAP and key management frames to the AC. It MAY bridge client data locally, or tunnel it to the AC using 802.3 frame tunnel mode or 802.11 frame tunnel mode.

In Split MAC, frames sent to the AC carry the 802.11 MAC header contents. When the WTP does the encryption, it MUST decrypt uplink frames, set the Protected Frame field to 0 and strip the added IV/EIV, MIC and ICV fields before sending to the AC. When the AC does the encryption, the WTP SHALL NOT decrypt uplink frames. The FCS field is not carried between WTP and AC: the WTP validates and strips it on uplink and adds it on downlink.

CAPWAP does not guarantee in-order delivery when tunneling data between WTP and AC. This is harmless for IP, but implementers need to be aware of it.
sections.eli5: Split MAC is like a shop where the clerk at the door only greets people and the manager in the back office decides everything else. In Local MAC the clerk handles more things and only asks the manager about the important ones.

sections.title: Joining, Roaming and Group Key Refresh
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, a station joins a WLAN with 802.1X authentication and AES-CCMP encryption. The WTP builds Beacons from the Add WLAN information and answers Probe Requests itself. The AC takes the Authentication and Association frames and then sends a Station Configuration Request carrying an Add Station element and an IEEE 802.11 Station Session Key element with the 'A' flag. After the 802.1X authentication and key exchange, the AC sends another Station Configuration Request. If the WTP encrypts, this includes the pairwise key and the RSN information element. If the AC encrypts, it sets the 'C' flag instead.

When a client roams from an old WTP to a new one, the AC repeats the same procedure with the new WTP and sends a Delete Station to the old one. If key caching is used, the 802.1X authentication step is skipped.

The group key (GTK) for the BSS needs to be updated periodically. The AC sends an IEEE 802.11 WLAN Configuration Request with an Update WLAN element and Key Status set to 3 (begin GTK update), then updates each station using EAPOL-Key frames. While that happens, broadcast frames are duplicated and sent under both the current and new key, by the AC in Split MAC or by the WTP in Local MAC. When done, the AC sends another Update WLAN with Key Status 4 (GTK update complete).

For BSSIDs, the WTP assigns them when a WLAN is created. The RFC advises assigning them as a contiguous block, for example base BSSID plus WLAN ID.
sections.eli5: When you walk from one wifi box to the next, the boss hands your pass to the new box and takes it back from the old one. When the secret password for group messages changes, the boss briefly shouts messages in both the old and new code so nobody misses out.

sections.title: QoS and Data Message Bindings
sections.content:
When a WLAN is created, a default QoS policy is set through the IEEE 802.11 WTP Quality of Service element. The AC MAY override it for one station with an Update Station QoS element. The Tagging Policy field uses bits to say how packets are marked: the 'P' bit selects 802.1p (with 'Q' choosing which priority values), and the 'D' bit selects DSCP marking (with 'I' and 'O' choosing the inner station packet, the outer tunnel header, or both). The AC MAY ask for none, one or both mechanisms. For MAC management frames the RFC recommends 802.1p precedence 7 (4 for Probe Requests) and the CS6 per-hop behavior for DSCP.

The CAPWAP data message carries the 802.11 header and payload, without the 802.11 FCS. In the optional Wireless Specific Information header, frames going from WTP to AC carry an IEEE 802.11 Frame Info field with radio details. Frames going from AC to WTP can carry a Destination WLANs field, used only for broadcast and multicast frames, so the AC sends one frame and the WTP replicates it to the chosen WLANs.
sections.eli5: Frames get priority stickers so important traffic like phone calls gets through first. Each frame from the wifi box also carries a little note about how strong the signal was.

sections.title: Control Messages and Message Elements
sections.content:
The binding defines two CAPWAP control messages, using IANA enterprise number 13277: IEEE 802.11 WLAN Configuration Request (3398913) and Response (3398914). The AC sends the request to create, update or delete a WLAN, with exactly one of Add WLAN, Delete WLAN or Update WLAN. The WTP replies with a Result Code, and may include the Assigned WTP BSSID. A WTP may serve several WLANs, each identified by an index. A WTP that supports up to 16 SSIDs could accept up to 16 requests with Add WLAN.

It also defines 25 IEEE 802.11 message elements, with type values 1024 to 1048. They cover the WLAN itself (Add, Update, Delete), radio settings (Antenna, Direct Sequence Control, OFDM Control, Tx Power, Rate Set, Supported Rates), per-station data (Station, Station QoS Profile, Station Session Key), and reporting (Statistics, MIC Countermeasures, RSNA Error Report, Radio Fail Alarm). Section 5 lists which of these may appear in the existing CAPWAP messages. For example, an IEEE 802.11 WTP Radio Information element MUST appear in the Discovery, Primary Discovery and Join messages for every radio in the WTP.

The Add WLAN element carries the Radio ID, a WLAN ID that MUST be between 1 and 16, a capability field, key data, QoS and authentication type, MAC mode, tunnel mode, SSID suppression and the SSID. It MUST be accompanied by Information Elements such as the RSN information element, which tells the WTP which cipher to use.
sections.eli5: The boss has a small set of note types for telling a wifi box 'start this network', 'change it' or 'remove it', plus lots of little forms for radio settings, and the box says 'done' or reports a problem.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With WEP, CAPWAP adds no new vulnerabilities, but WEP session keys can be compromised, so implementers SHOULD discourage WEP and encourage an IEEE 802.11 RSN. Station authentication uses 802.1X and therefore EAP, and implementers SHOULD use EAP methods meeting the requirements of RFC 4017.

With RSN, link security provided by the AC introduces no new concerns. When the WTP provides it, there is a new, narrow weakness. If other clients are already associated and broadcast traffic has been sent under the existing GTK, the AC does not know the exact receive sequence counter (KeyRSC) when it builds message 3 of the 4-way handshake. A new client may therefore accept replayed older broadcast or multicast traffic until it sees a valid frame. The RFC expects the window to be very small on busy networks and replays to be detectable and loggable by the WTP. It accepts this as a calculated risk, and says the AC SHOULD use an RSC of 0 unless it knows a better value.
sections.eli5: There is one small gap: a newcomer might briefly believe an old group message that someone replays. The authors decided the gap is tiny and not worth a more complicated fix.
